agent.problem: Four of the six choice cards (2, 4, 6 and 8) require the baker to pick unseen content without enough basis in the earlier cards: whether the blessed person has never sinned, which inner quality he has, which bodily symptom David suffered and which seasonal simile David used. Only cards 9 and 10 are clearly reasoned from the setup, so this stop relies more on discovery guesses than informed guesses.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer. The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

agent.problem: The card makes the baker guess an unseen wording detail: whether David's simile concerns summer heat or winter cold. Like guessing what David's head was anointed with in the document's example, this tests an incidental detail rather than the movement or meaning of the poetry.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says. Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

agent.problem: Cards 9 and 10 have already covered David's confession and the LORD's forgiveness. This card restates that same material with a joke rather than advancing through the psalm, making it a recap card.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage. No recap cards.

agent.problem: The card quotes the first-person words "I will instruct you" but introduces them only as a promise made by "the psalm." It never identifies who is speaking.

rule.text: When he quotes someone speaking as "I," he says who it is first.

agent.problem: "Right after that promise" points back to story card 6, which is no longer on screen. The question needs to supply the promise's context itself rather than referring to it as "that promise."

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

human.problem: Verse 8 is spoken as 'I', but the text does not say who is speaking: God or David. The card avoids naming anyone and says 'the psalm makes a promise'.
human.question: The 'Who's speaking' rule says to name the speaker before quoting an 'I' line. 'Leave open what the text leaves open' only names who is being spoken to. When the text itself leaves the speaker open, as in Psalm 32:8, should Papa Dorin name a speaker, or is a neutral 'the psalm says' the right way to do it?

human.problem: Verse 8 is quoted with "I" ("I will instruct you…") without saying who is speaking. The card says only "the psalm makes a promise". The text doesn't say whether the speaker is the LORD or David.
human.question: The "Who's speaking" rule says to name the speaker before an "I" quote, but "Leave open what the text leaves open" says not to settle who is speaking when the text doesn't. When the speaker of an "I" line is unclear in the text, as in Psalm 32:8, should Papa Dorin name a speaker, or is a neutral lead-in like "the psalm makes a promise" acceptable?
